The history of technology is the record of the invention of tools and techniques. This is one of the categories of world history. Technology can refer to the earliest simple stone tools of prehistory or the complex genetic engineering and information technology that has emerged since the 1980s. The term technology comes from the Greek words techne, meaning art and craft, and  logos, meaning word and speech. It was first used to describe applied arts, but now it describes advancements and changes affecting our environment. Before modern humans (Homo sapiens sapiens) evolved, early humans invented stone tools, huts, and hand axes. Then Homo erectus learned to master and use fire as early as 1.5 million years ago. Next, they invented boats (900,000 years ago), then cooking (500,000 years ago), and javelins (400,000 years ago). Modern humans evolved 100,000 years later.

Many sociologists and anthropologists have created social and cultural evolution theories. Some, like Lewis Morgan, Leslie White, and Gerhard Lenski, have declared technological progress to be the primary factor driving human progress. Morgan suggests three stages of social evolution: savagery, barbarism, and civilization. These can be divided by milestones, like the use of fire. White argued that energy was the measure to judge the evolution of culture. The main function of culture is to "harness and control energy." White outlines five stages of human development. First, people use the energy of their own muscles. Second, they use the energy of tamed animals. Third, they use the energy of plants through farming. Fourth, they use energy from natural resources like coal, oil, and gas. Fifth, they harness nuclear energy. Lenski focuses on information. He states there are four stages. Information is passed through genes, then individual experience, followed by symbols, and finally language.

Stone Age cultures developed music and engaged in organized warfare. Stone Age humans advanced ocean-worthy outrigger canoe technology. This led to migration across the Indian Ocean to Madagascar. People also sailed across the Pacific Ocean. This feat required ocean currents, weather patterns, sailing, and celestial navigation knowledge. Paleolithic cultures left no written records. Despite this, the shift from nomadic life to settlement and agriculture can be inferred. There is a range of archaeological evidence. Such evidence includes ancient tools, cave paintings, and other prehistoric art. One example of art is the Venus of Willendorf. Human remains also provide evidence. We can examine bones and study mummies. Historians have been able to form strong guesses about the lifestyle and culture of prehistoric peoples. That includes their technology. The Copper, Bronze, and Iron Ages advanced new techniques for smelting and forging. This helped create more art, tools, and weapons.

Mesopotamia is modern Iraq. The Sumerians, Akkadians, Assyrians, and Babylonians all created empires here. They developed cities by 4000 BCE. Cities were built with sophisticated architecture in mud-brick and stone, including the use of the true arch. The walls of Babylon were so massive they were quoted as a Wonder of the World. They developed extensive water systems, including catchment systems and canals for transport and irrigation, and their palaces had sophisticated drainage systems. Several of the six classical simple machines were invented here. The wheel, axle, and potter’s wheel arrived in 5000 BCE. Wheeled vehicles came to the scene in 4000 BCE. They invented levers, pulleys, and screws. They used bronze technology for tools, weapons, and statues. Most vital to transferring knowledge, they invented writing, using the cuneiform script, and many records on clay tablets and stone inscriptions have survived. For over 800 years, they tracked the stars and kept diaries.
